content.title: Wireless Network Access Control Requirements
content.original_description: Build a campus wireless network access-control requirements specification. Students and guests may access the internet but must not access the internal staff network. Network administrators may manually isolate a device and restore its access. Security operators may review and acknowledge alerts but may not change access policies. The system must record administrator policy changes and retain audit records for 30 days. The planning population is 2000 registered devices; concurrency is not yet decided. Do not automatically change firewall rules or isolate devices. Requirements evolve frequently and stakeholders provide weekly stakeholder feedback. Budget, delivery schedule, response-time thresholds and mandatory regulatory frameworks are undecided and must remain open decisions.

analysis.title: Wireless Network Access Control Requirements
analysis.summary: A campus wireless network must enforce access control such that students and guests may access the internet but not internal staff networks. Administrators can manually isolate devices, and security operators can review alerts without altering policies. Policy changes are logged for 30 days. No automatic isolation or firewall rule changes are permitted. Requirements evolve frequently with weekly stakeholder feedback; budget, delivery schedule, response thresholds, and regulatory compliance remain open decisions.

assessments.explanation: The project purpose is to build a campus wireless network access-control specification.
Students and guests may access the internet but must not access internal staff networks, establishing clear boundary rules for access control.
Network administrators may manually isolate a device and restore its access, defining an exception path with explicit administrative authority.
Security operators may review and acknowledge alerts but may not change access policies, restricting operator permissions to monitoring only.
The system must record administrator policy changes and retain audit records for 30 days, establishing a data retention requirement with audit purpose.
The planning population is 2000 registered devices; concurrency is not yet decided, indicating current scale limits but no defined performance targets.
Do not automatically change firewall rules or isolate devices, prohibiting automated actions and restricting to manual control only.
Requirements evolve frequently with weekly stakeholder feedback, indicating a dynamic requirements lifecycle but no defined evolution mechanism.
Budget, delivery schedule, response thresholds, and regulatory compliance remain open decisions, indicating these are project-level constraints, not system behaviors.

### 4. Access is Determined by Dynamic Policy

Access decisions consider multiple factors: who's asking, what device they're using, where they're connecting from, what time it is, and how they normally behave. These policies change based on risk. Someone accessing payroll during work hours from their work laptop is low risk. The same person downloading lots of data at 2 AM from a coffee shop is high risk.

### 5. Monitor and Measure the Security Posture of All Assets

Continuously check the health and security of all devices and systems. If you can't see it, you can't protect it. This includes monitoring for patches, antivirus status, configuration changes, and suspicious behavior. Assets that fall out of compliance lose access.

### 6. All Authentication and Authorization is Dynamic and Strictly Enforced

Security decisions happen in real-time for every access request. Don't rely on static rules or permanent permissions. The system should automatically adjust access based on current risk levels, revoke access for compromised accounts, and isolate suspicious devices.

### 7. Collect Information to Improve Security Posture

Gather as much security data as possible about users, devices, network traffic, and system behavior. Use this information to detect threats, improve policies, and make better security decisions. This data is essential for compliance and incident investigation.

- **Certificate-based device identity**: Use PKI certificates to uniquely identify and authenticate each device
- **Vulnerability scanning**: Regular assessment of device security posture and patch levels
- **Revoke trust when compromised**: Automatically remove access if device security is compromised

### Protecting Endpoints

Every device needs these protections:

- **Anti-malware software**: Real-time protection against viruses and malware
- **Behavior monitoring**: Watch for suspicious device activity
- **Full disk encryption**: Encrypt all data on the device
- **Remote wipe**: Ability to erase lost or stolen devices

## Network Architecture

### Micro-Segmentation

Instead of one big network, create small isolated segments:

- **Separate by application**: Each app gets its own network segment
- **Block by default**: Don't allow traffic unless specifically permitted
- **Monitor internal traffic**: Watch data moving between systems
- **Use encrypted communications**: All communication between systems must be encrypted

### Network Controls

Implement these network protections:

- **DNS filtering**: Block access to malicious websites
- **Web filtering**: Control what websites users can visit
- **Replace VPNs**: Use Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) instead
- **Monitor traffic**: Analyze all network connections

## Application and Data Protection

### Securing Applications

Protect your applications with these controls:

- **Identity-aware proxy**: Check user identity before allowing app access
- **Web Application Firewalls (WAFs)**: Block OWASP Top 10 attacks at the application layer. Deploy at network edge, internal segments, or as part of API gateways

An example of such segmentation:
![Interservice Communication with balancing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OWASP/CheatSheetSeries/master/assets/Network_Segmentation_Cheat_Sheet_interservice_balancer.drawio.png)

As you can see, there is only one incoming access to each network, access is opened up to the balancer in the network. However, in this case, segmentation no longer works, access control between applications from different network segments is performed at the 7th level of the OSI model using a balancer.

## Network security policy

The organization must define a "paper" policy that describes firewall rules and basic allowed network access.
This policy is at least useful:

- network administrators;
- security representatives;
- IT auditors;
- architects of information systems and software;
- developers;
- IT administrators.

It is convenient when the policy is described by similar images. The information is presented as concisely and simply as possible.

### Examples of individual policy provisions

Examples in the network policy will help colleagues quickly understand what access is potentially allowed and can be requested.

#### Permissions for CI/CD

**Secure applications properly** - Add identity-aware proxies and web application firewalls (WAFs) that make security decisions based on who's trying to access what, not just where they're connecting from.

### Phase 3: Advanced Capabilities (Months 18-36)

Build advanced capabilities:

**Add behavior monitoring** - Use systems that learn how users and devices normally act. When behavior looks weird, the system can automatically change access or ask for more verification. This needs machine learning and lots of data.

**Automate responses** - Build tools that can automatically isolate compromised accounts, quarantine suspicious devices, and update security policies based on new threats. The goal is to respond faster than humans can.

**Use your data** - Take all the security data you're collecting and use it to improve your policies. This phase is about fine-tuning rather than building new stuff.

### Phase 4: Keep Getting Better (Ongoing)

Zero Trust is never done:

**Stay current** - Update threat intelligence, adjust risk scoring, and change policies based on new attack methods. What worked last year might not work now.

**Plan ahead** - Start thinking about post-quantum cryptography, new authentication methods, and AI-powered security tools.

**Measure what matters** - Track how fast you detect threats, how fast you respond, how many policy violations happen, and whether users are happy. Use this data to keep improving.

**Reality check:** Most organizations take 3-5 years to fully implement Zero Trust, and that's with dedicated teams and management support. Don't expect quick resul

## Technology Components

Zero Trust requires several technology categories working together:

- **Identity and Access Management**: Strong authentication (MFA) and risk-based access decisions
- **Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)**: Application-level access instead of network-level VPNs
- **Web Application Security**: Protect applications and APIs from OWASP Top 10 attacks
- **Security Monitoring**: Real-time visibility and automated response to threats

### Policy-as-Code + Continuous Verification + Telemetry Signals

#### 1. Policy-as-Code (PaC)

Zero Trust policies should be defined as **code**, not manually, ensuring consistency, reproducibility, and auditability.

**Key principles:**

- Version-controlled policies
- Tested within CI/CD pipelines
- Automatically enforced at deployment
- Traceable via audit logs

**Recommended tools:**

- Open Policy Agent (OPA) / Gatekeeper
- Kyverno
- Cilium Network Policies
- Cloud provider policy engines (AWS SCP, Azure Policy, GCP Org Policy)

**Use cases:**

- Admission control
- Workload security (privileges, capabilities, runtime profiles)
- Network segmentation (L3–L7)
- Image and artifact security
- RBAC enforcement

Refer to [CISA's "Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks"](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/avoiding-social-engineering-and-phishing-attacks) for guidance.

## Adaptive or Risk Based Authentication

A feature of more advanced applications is the ability to require different authentication stages depending on various environmental and contextual attributes (including but not limited to, the sensitivity of the data for which access is being requested, time of day, user location, IP address, or device fingerprint).

For example, an application may require MFA for the first login from a particular device but not for subsequent logins from that device. Alternatively, a single sign-on solution may authenticate the user and allow them to remain logged in for a day but require a reauthentication if they try to access their profile page.

Another option is the opposite approach where an application allows low risk access with just something that identifies the device (e.g., a specific mobile device fingerprint, a persistent cookie and browser fingerprint, etc. from the previous IP address) and then gradually requires stronger authentication for more sensitive operations. An example might be to allow someone to trigger something to see their current bank balance, but not the account number or anything else. If they need to see transactions, then the application puts them through some base level authentication and if they want to do any money movement, then MFA is required.

requirements.title: Students and guests may access the internet but must not access the internal staff network
requirements.statement: Students and guests may access the internet but must not access the internal staff network.
requirements.rationale: This establishes a clear boundary between public-facing internet access and restricted internal staff network access, ensuring that unauthorized users do not gain entry to sensitive internal systems.

acceptance_criteria.given: A student or guest is authenticated and connected to the wireless network using a valid public identity.
acceptance_criteria.when: The user attempts to access the internet via standard web browsing services.
acceptance_criteria.then: The system allows successful access to publicly available internet content.
acceptance_criteria.observable_evidence: Record of successful page load from a public website, such as google.com.

acceptance_criteria.given: A student or guest is authenticated and connected to the wireless network using a valid public identity.
acceptance_criteria.when: The user attempts to access internal staff network resources via IP address or domain name (e.g., internal.staff.company.com).
acceptance_criteria.then: The system denies access and no product message is returned; traffic is blocked as evidenced by an external test capture of the network response state.
acceptance_criteria.observable_evidence: Export of a test-instrumented network response state capture showing denied access to internal staff network resources, captured at the time of request and verified against known firewall rule enforcement.

unresolved_decisions: Whether the system must enforce this boundary at the application layer or only via network-level filtering.
The specific mechanism for detecting and blocking attempts to reach internal staff network resources.

requirements.title: Network administrators may manually isolate a device and restore its access
requirements.statement: Network administrators may manually isolate a device and restore its access.
requirements.rationale: This action defines an explicit administrative exception path for device management, allowing manual intervention when necessary without requiring automated or policy-driven isolation mechanisms.

acceptance_criteria.given: A network administrator logs into the system with valid administrative credentials.
acceptance_criteria.when: The administrator selects a device to isolate via the manual isolation interface.
acceptance_criteria.then: The system isolates the device from wireless access and updates the access control state accordingly.
acceptance_criteria.observable_evidence: Capture the system response state after manual isolation via API call and validate it against expected access control update.

acceptance_criteria.given: A network administrator logs into the system with valid administrative credentials.
acceptance_criteria.when: The administrator selects a device that has been isolated to restore access via the manual restoration interface.
acceptance_criteria.then: The system restores wireless access for the device and updates the access control state accordingly.
acceptance_criteria.observable_evidence: Capture the system response state after manual restoration of wireless access for the device, including the updated access control state and the timestamp of the action.

unresolved_decisions: The specific interface or UI component used for isolation and restoration is not defined; this remains an implementation parameter.

requirements.title: Do not automatically change firewall rules or isolate devices
requirements.statement: The system shall not automatically change firewall rules or isolate devices.
requirements.rationale: Explicitly prohibits automated actions such as isolation or rule modification, ensuring that all such operations are performed manually by authorized personnel.

acceptance_criteria.given: The system is configured to automatically modify firewall rules or isolate a device in response to an event
acceptance_criteria.when: An automated action such as rule modification or isolation is initiated by the system
acceptance_criteria.then: The action shall be denied and no change to firewall configuration or device state shall occur
acceptance_criteria.observable_evidence: Capture of unchanged firewall configuration and unmodified device state before and after the attempted action

requirements.title: Security operators shall be permitted to review and acknowledge alerts
requirements.statement: Security operators may review and acknowledge alerts but may not change access policies.
requirements.rationale: The source passage explicitly states that security operators may review and acknowledge alerts but may not modify access policies, which defines their authorized actions in the system.

acceptance_criteria.given: A security operator accesses an alert dashboard
acceptance_criteria.when: The operator views a network anomaly report
acceptance_criteria.then: The operator can acknowledge the alert and receive confirmation of acknowledgment
acceptance_criteria.observable_evidence: Record of acknowledged alert with timestamp and operator identity

acceptance_criteria.given: An operator receives an alert with a visible status indicator.
acceptance_criteria.when: The operator reviews the alert and acknowledges it via the system interface.
acceptance_criteria.then: The system updates the alert status to 'acknowledged' and retains the original policy unchanged; no policy modification occurs.
acceptance_criteria.observable_evidence: Capture of the system response showing alert status updated to 'acknowledged' with no change in access policies, as verified by a test-instrumented state capture of the alert object's properties.

acceptance_criteria.given: A security operator receives an alert with a policy violation.
acceptance_criteria.when: The operator attempts to modify an access policy through the system interface.
acceptance_criteria.then: The system denies the modification request and returns a response indicating that policy modifications are not permitted for operators.
acceptance_criteria.observable_evidence: Capture of the system's direct response shows a denial of the modification action, with no change to the access policies in storage or configuration.

requirements.title: The system shall record administrator policy changes and retain audit records for 30 days
requirements.statement: The system shall record administrator policy changes and retain audit records for 30 days.
requirements.rationale: Establishes a data retention requirement with an audit purpose to ensure accountability and traceability of administrative actions affecting network access policies.

acceptance_criteria.given: An administrator modifies a network access policy, such as changing authentication requirements or access permissions.
acceptance_criteria.when: The system records the change and stores it in an audit log.
acceptance_criteria.then: The audit record is retained for 30 days and remains accessible for review by authorized personnel.
acceptance_criteria.observable_evidence: Inspect the audit log to confirm that a policy change event was recorded with timestamp, actor identity, action type, and before/after state.

procedure: Given: A student or guest is authenticated and connected to the wireless network using a valid public identity.
When: The user attempts to access internal staff network resources via IP address or domain name (e.g., internal.staff.company.com).

tests.evidence_to_record: Evidence: Export of a test-instrumented network response state capture showing denied access to internal staff network resources, captured at the time of request and verified against known firewall rule enforcement.

procedure: Given: A network administrator logs into the system with valid administrative credentials.
When: The administrator selects a device to isolate via the manual isolation interface.
tests.expected_result: Expected: The system isolates the device from wireless access and updates the access control state accordingly.
tests.evidence_to_record: Evidence: Capture the system response state after manual isolation via API call and validate it against expected access control update.

procedure: Given: A network administrator logs into the system with valid administrative credentials.
When: The administrator selects a device that has been isolated to restore access via the manual restoration interface.
tests.expected_result: Expected: The system restores wireless access for the device and updates the access control state accordingly.
tests.evidence_to_record: Evidence: Capture the system response state after manual restoration of wireless access for the device, including the updated access control state and the timestamp of the action.

tests.expected_result: Expected: The action shall be denied and no change to firewall configuration or device state shall occur
tests.evidence_to_record: Evidence: Capture of unchanged firewall configuration and unmodified device state before and after the attempted action

glossary.summary: Source-present terminology; definitions introduce no additional product obligation.

items.title: Access control
items.detail: Rules and enforcement governing which principals may perform actions on resources.

items.title: Policy
items.detail: A rule or decision governing permitted actions; its project-specific meaning remains defined by the source requirements.

items.title: Audit record
items.detail: A stored record of an event. Required event scope and retention are determined by the linked source, not this definition.

items.title: Device isolation
items.detail: Restriction of a device's network access; the source determines whether and by whom this action is permitted.

items.title: Access restoration
items.detail: Returning access that was previously restricted, within the source-defined permission boundary.

items.title: Concurrency
items.detail: Activity occurring at the same time; it is distinct from the registered planning population.

items.title: Registered population
items.detail: The inventory of registered users or devices; it does not by itself establish a simultaneous load or a maximum.

items.title: Retention
items.detail: The period or rule for keeping records. A bare duration does not itself specify deletion timing or minimum/maximum bounds.

items.title: Firewall
items.detail: A control that permits or restricts network traffic according to rules; mentioning it does not authorize automatic changes.
